newsitem.title: LEBANON: ESCWA region 1997 GDP growth seen down to 3.7 pct.
newsitem.headline: ESCWA region 1997 GDP growth seen down to 3.7 pct.

text.p: Economic growth among the 13 members of the U.N's Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia will slow to 3.7 percent in 1997 from 4.3 percent in 1996, an ESCWA report said.
It called the projected growth for the region "fairly positive" despite the slowdown. This compared with 2.1 percent growth in 1995.

The preliminary report, distributed at ESCWA's 19th bi-annual ministerial meeting which opened in Beirut on Wednesday, covered Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen.
"Although the outlook for the ESCWA region as a whole for 1997 is not as good as in 1996, it remains fairly positive," it said.
Syria led the region with 5.9 percent growth in 1996, followed by Kuwait with 5.7 percent and Oman and Jordan with 5.2 percent.

Egypt's economy grew 4.9 percent, Yemen 4.8 percent, Lebanon four percent and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries grew at an average 4.1 percent, the report said. It did not give growth rates for Iraq or the Palestinian self-rule areas.
World oil prices, economic reforms by member countries and the Middle East process would greatly affect the region's economic performance in 1997, the report said.
"Positive developments (in the peace process) would encourage foreign and domestic investment and increase revenues from tourism," it said.
Israel's peace talks with the Palestinians and with Syria and Lebanon are currently stalled.
The report said oil prices were expected to fall below 1996's $20 per barrel.
"This will significantly affect the GCC countries. It would reduce their balance of trade surpluses, widen their budget deficits and reduce the growth of the non-oil sectors," it said.
On economic reform, it said Bahrain, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates reduced their budget deficit ratios to GDP to less than 1.5 percent in 1996, according to preliminary estimates.
Estimated ratios for ESCWA countries excluding Iraq, Syria and the Palestinian areas ranged between 0.2 percent for the UAE and 4.6 percent for Jordan. Lebanon was an estimated 14 percent.
ESCWA said unemployment was a regional problem with the increase in demand for labour failing to absorb the increase in supply in recent years.
The highest rate was 28 percent in the West Bank and Gaza Strip caused by high population growth and Israel's border closures.
It was 25 percent in Yemen and 13 percent in Egypt and Jordan. No rate was given for Syria but the report said it was lower than Egypt and Jordan.
However, inflation rates in ESCAW countries stood at "internationally acceptable levels" in 1996 and were not expected to change much in 1997.
